title: 5 Habits to Hear God Daily
hook: Want to hear God more clearly? Do these 5 things.
script: Want to hear God more clearly? Do these 5 things. Jesus said, 'My sheep hear my voice' (John 10:27). Here’s how to train your ears. First, open Scripture before your phone; His Word is a lamp to your feet (Psalm 119:105). Second, sit in five minutes of silence—breathe and become aware that He is near. Third, pray surrendered prayers: 'Father, not my will, but Yours' (Luke 22:42). Fourth, journal what you sense and then test it; keep what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Fifth, share it with wise believers who stir you toward love (Hebrews 10:24–25). Do this daily, even when it feels quiet. Patterns form, anxiety drops, and His guidance grows clear.

title: The 7-Day 10-10-10 Challenge
hook: If God feels silent right now, watch this.
script: If God feels silent right now, watch this. For the next 7 days, try the 10-10-10. Ten minutes in the Word—let Psalm 119:105 guide your reading. Ten minutes of silence—no music, just breathing and being with God. Ten minutes of journaling—pray Luke 22:42, write what surfaces, then test it by 1 Thessalonians 5:21. Close by texting a mature friend for feedback—Hebrews 10:24-25. Set a timer, same place, same hour. In one week your anxiety lowers, your mind quiets, and patterns of His voice emerge. Start tomorrow morning. Simple, consistent, expectant. You’re not chasing a feeling—you’re training to recognize your Shepherd.

title: Stop Overthinking: Safely Discern God's Voice
script: You may be overthinking this. God’s voice isn’t a code to crack; it’s a Shepherd to follow (John 10:27). Use these guardrails. What you hear will agree with Scripture and move you toward love and holiness. It brings steady peace, not frantic pressure. It stands up to time and wise counsel. Try this today: five minutes of silence, pray Luke 22:42, write what you sense, then wait 24 hours. Re-read with your Bible open. Share it with a mature friend. If it still rings true, take the next small obedient step. Clarity often comes while you’re walking, not while you’re worrying.
